analysis.one_liner: Preserves state lawsuits against pesticide makers over inadequate product warnings.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 29, 2026 with one Republican cosponsor and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal pesticide law requires that labels and warnings for pesticides be approved nationally. Pesticide makers have used that system in court to argue that people cannot sue them under state law for failing to warn about dangers like cancer. This bill writes into the law that those state lawsuits over labeling or packaging stay alive, so someone harmed by a pesticide can still take the maker to court.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to pesticides — farmworkers, commercial applicators, gardeners, and rural residents — who are harmed by inadequate warnings and want to hold the manufacturer accountable in their own state's courts. Roughly the people behind the thousands of suits over the weed-killer glyphosate would keep their day in court.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the section of the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) that governs state authority, adding that nothing in it may be read to bar or limit a state tort claim about the labeling or packaging of pesticides [S2].
The stated purpose is to protect tort claims under state law related to pesticide labeling or packaging — the lawsuits manufacturers argue are wiped out by federal label approval [S2].
The short title, 'People Over Poison Act,' frames the change as putting people exposed to pesticides ahead of the products that harm them [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers, who would lose their strongest courtroom defense — that federal label approval preempts state failure-to-warn suits — and would face verdicts and settlements in state courts. Some of that cost could be passed through to farmers and other pesticide users.

drawbacks.text: The industry's good-faith objection is that FIFRA exists to create one uniform, federally approved label nationwide, and letting every state's tort law demand different warnings would make national labeling impossible; this is exactly the conflict the bill's amendment walks into [S2].

Because the bill only preserves existing state-law claims and adds no new federal safety standard, it increases litigation without itself making pesticides any safer — accountability, but not prevention [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: people who say a pesticide's warning was inadequate get to use state courts rather than lose on a technical preemption defense. The cost falls on manufacturers, and the counterargument — that uniform federal labels are the point of the statute — is serious enough that Congress has not enacted this protection in decades of litigation. The bill is narrow and honest about what it does, but it settles a multi-billion-dollar question in favor of plaintiffs by legislative flat rather than adjudication.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced June 29, 2026 and sent straight to the House Agriculture Committee, where it has sat since with no hearing, no markup, and no vote as the session runs down [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME) introduced the bill on June 29, 2026 [S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture, which holds jurisdiction over federal pesticide law [S1].
One Republican, Rep. Thomas Massie, cosponsored it; the action history shows no further steps after the referral [S3].
The bill text is a single amendment to FIFRA Section 24(b) preserving state tort claims over pesticide labeling or packaging [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, pesticide manufacturers. With the bill stalled in committee and the session ending in early January 2027, they keep the federal preemption defense that state-court lawsuits over pesticide warnings must clear. People exposed to pesticides have gained nothing yet.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two supporters are one Democrat (Pingree) and one Republican (Massie), and no vote was ever scheduled, so the chamber's parties never took a position on it.

industries.note: The bill strips away the argument that federal label approval shields them from state failure-to-warn lawsuits, reopening manufacturers to liability in state courts. Their interest in keeping that shield runs directly against the interests of people harmed by inadequate warnings.

As the people who handle pesticides, farmers and applicators would gain a way to sue over bad warnings, but manufacturers could pass litigation costs into pesticide prices. Their interest mostly tracks the public's, with a price edge.

analysis.trajectory: With roughly six months left in the session, a single amendment bill with two cosponsors sitting in the Agriculture Committee without a hearing almost never reaches the floor; expect it to die quietly at the end of this Congress unless attached to a larger package.
